Fable 5 Is the First Model You Have to Tell When to Stop

Anthropic just put a Mythos-class model in public hands. The benchmarks are real, the autonomy is genuinely new, and the catch shows up on your invoice. A researched review, weighted toward the people who actually ran it.

Anthropic released Claude Fable 5 on June 9, and it is the most capable model the public can use right now. That part is not in dispute. What makes it worth a real review, rather than a benchmark screenshot, is the shape of the thing. Fable 5 is not a smarter answer to a single question. It is a model built to keep going for days, and the single most useful sentence written about it so far came from Zapier: "Where Opus stops to ask, Fable 5 keeps looking."

That trait is the whole story, the good half and the bad half. It is why Fable can collapse a month of work into an afternoon. It is also why it will quietly run until something cuts it off, which makes it slow and roughly twice the price of Opus 4.8. You do not get one without the other.

Three things to take away:

  • Fable 5 leads nearly every coding, knowledge-work, and computer-use benchmark, and the gap is widest on long, messy, multi-step work rather than single prompts. On SWE-bench Pro it clears the field by 11 points, which is not a normal release-to-release delta.
  • Its defining trait is autonomy. It keeps working where older models stop and check in. That is the product, and it is also the failure mode, because it does not know when it is finished. Judge it by cost per solved task, not by the per-token rate.
  • Reach for it on genuinely long jobs that deserve a thorough result: migrations, deep research, agent harnesses with clear stop conditions. For quick edits, high-volume code review, or anything latency-sensitive, Opus 4.8 is still the smarter default.

What it actually is

Anthropic ships its frontier capability in two forms. Mythos 5 is the unrestricted version, handed to vetted users with the cybersecurity safeguards lifted. Fable 5 is the same underlying model with the guardrails switched on, released to everyone on Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans. Both sit in a tier the company calls Mythos-class, which it places a step above the Opus line.

The pitch is endurance, not raw IQ. Fable 5 is built to run for days, planning across stages, spawning sub-agents, and checking its own work. It carries a one million token context window and a new file-based memory it uses to jot notes mid-task and refer back to them later, which matters more than the context number on long runs. The headline proof point came from Stripe, which reports Fable completed a migration across a 50 million line Ruby codebase in a single day, work a team had scoped at more than two months by hand.

The numbers

These are the figures Anthropic published, with several cross-checked against independent aggregators like Vellum, DataCamp, and Artificial Analysis. Treat any vendor benchmark as a ceiling rather than a promise. The deltas here are still large enough to mean something.

The coding results are the clearest. Fable hits 95 percent on SWE-bench Verified, leads SWE-bench Pro by 11 points, and more than doubles Opus on the hardest FrontierCode Diamond set. Two non-coding numbers stand out as much. On GDPval-AA, a benchmark of real economic knowledge-work tasks, Fable scores 1932 and takes the top spot, well ahead of Gemini 3.1 Pro at 1314. And it is the first model to break 90 percent on a core long-running analytics benchmark, a 10 point jump over Opus. Artificial Analysis put it first on its Intelligence Index, roughly 5 points clear of any other lab's best. The pattern holds across all of it: the longer and more tool-heavy the task, the wider Fable's lead.

Real-world use

Benchmarks rhyme with the hands-on reports here, which is not always the case. The clearest independent read comes from Simon Willison, who spent about five and a half hours putting it through actual work.

The moment that stuck was not a benchmark. He asked Fable to add a feature to one of his projects, and it did, then went on to find and fix four separate issues in his underlying library that he had not mentioned. He called the model "something of a beast" and said the harder challenge was finding tasks it could not do. That captures the real shift. The standout is not the quality of one answer, it is how much ground it covers without being told to.

The named customers describe the same thing from different angles. Notion turned a pile of messy notes into a working project plan in a single pass. Hebbia logged its highest-ever score on a finance benchmark, and the trading firm IMC said Fable cleared their analysis evaluations almost across the board. Vision is part of this rather than a bolt-on. Fable reads charts, tables, and PDFs, and it uses sight to check its own coding work against an original design. In one independent test it rebuilt a Netflix page from a screenshot and turned a hand-drawn wireframe into a working React dashboard, filling in the missing colors, spacing, and interaction with sensible defaults.

That same test carried the caveat you hear everywhere. Some of the output, the reviewer noted, leaned toward extra styling that would need refinement for production. Fable gets you most of the way, not all of it, and the last stretch is still yours.

The autonomy that makes it impressive is also what makes it expensive. It tends to run until something stops it. Willison spent 110 dollars in a single day of ordinary use. The model is slow next to Opus, and in an agent loop without firm stop rules it will keep going long after a cheaper model would have called it done. None of that is a dealbreaker. It is a planning constraint. You set the budget and the stop condition, or the model sets them for you.

Coding

This is where Fable is most obviously ahead, and where the tradeoffs cut deepest. The benchmark wins are real, and so is the field reaction. Cursor calls it state of the art on its internal CursorBench and says it opened up a class of long-horizon problems that were out of reach. GitHub shipped it into Copilot on day one, citing autonomy and reliability that exceeded their previous benchmarks. Cognition reports it as the highest-scoring model on FrontierCode even at medium effort.

The most useful coding read is from CodeRabbit, because it is not a fan letter. They ran Fable two ways, as an autonomous builder and as a code reviewer, and got opposite results. As a builder it shines. From vague prompts it ships complete projects rather than prototype shells, explores the environment and its tools before writing anything, and produces real architecture across files with proper layering and working production builds. As a reviewer it slips. Its precision came in below Opus 4.8, 32.8 percent against 35.5, with more nitpicky output and weaker performance on the hardest cases. And the stopping problem showed up hard: 19 of 33 coding tasks ran to timeout rather than converging.

CodeRabbit's conclusion is the practical one. Keep Opus 4.8 as your default code reviewer, and reach for Fable 5 on autonomous build projects that have a clear time budget and an explicit stop condition. That maps exactly onto the cost story. Fable is not the model you fire at a one-line fix. It is the model you point at a migration or a greenfield feature and let run, with guardrails, because the thorough result is worth the longer, pricier session.

If you do put it on code, a few rules keep it honest. Give it a stop condition every time, a turn cap or a budget ceiling or a "done when tests pass" check, because left open it will keep going. Pay for prompt caching, since the 90 percent discount on cached input materially changes the math on long agent runs. Default to Opus for the small stuff. And measure cost per solved task, not the rate card. On the hard, long jobs Fable wins on that metric even at double the price. On the easy ones it loses badly.

What it costs you

Fable runs 10 dollars per million input tokens and 50 dollars per million output, double Opus 4.8 on both. Because it produces a lot of output and runs long, the effective bill climbs faster than the rate suggests. That is the one thing to internalize before you turn it loose. The 90 percent caching discount on input takes some of the edge off, but output volume is the real cost driver, and Fable generates plenty.

The flip side is that for genuinely hard, long-horizon work it can compress weeks into a day, and on cost per finished outcome that is a bargain. Both things are true at once. Which one you actually experience comes down to whether you point it at work that needs it.

Safety, briefly

Because the underlying model is Mythos-class, Fable 5 ships with a two-stage classifier that reroutes prompts touching cybersecurity, biology, chemistry, and health to Opus 4.8 instead. Anthropic says this catches fewer than 5 percent of sessions, and rerouted requests are not billed at Fable rates. A 30-day data retention requirement applies for safety monitoring, worth knowing if you operate under strict data-handling rules.

Bottom line

Fable 5 is the strongest model the public can use, and on the long, ambiguous, tool-heavy work that looks like an actual job rather than a quiz, the lead is not subtle. The honest reservation is not about capability. It is about discipline. The model does not know when it is finished, so you have to tell it, with budgets and stop conditions, or the bill writes the review for you.

Treat it as a specialist you bring in for the hard, long jobs. Give it guardrails. Aimed that way, it earns its rate easily. Aimed at everything, it will quietly drain your account proving it could have done the small stuff too.
